proposition: Every paying-guest owner is playing the same unwinnable level — verification, rent day, runners, reconciliation, complaints — and installing RentOK is the cheat code that clears it.

board.style_line: Flat 16-bit side-view pixel-art video-game frame, 9:16 vertical, chunky 24px sprite grid, hard-edged dithering, no anti-aliased gradients, one warm overhead source from a stairwell skylight, original artwork in an Indian paying-guest building —
board.negative_line: — no text, no letters, no numerals, no signage glyphs, no logos, no watermarks, no UI chrome, no Nintendo or Mario character, costume, artwork, font or asset, no plumber, no red cap, no coin or mushroom iconography, no weapons, no photoreal faces, no motion blur, no lens flare.

identity_anchors.OWNER: a stocky Indian man about forty-five in a tucked-in half-sleeve checked shirt and dark trousers, thick black moustache, reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, a small cloth pouch at his waist, drawn as a chunky 16-bit side-view sprite four heads tall
identity_anchors.PG_STAIRWELL: the open concrete stairwell of a four-storey Indian paying-guest building: half-landings, a painted steel handrail entering frame bottom-left and leaving top-right, room doors with small enamel number plates, a wall-mounted water cooler, a slipper rack, a room-number whiteboard, all flat 16-bit pixel art in a four-value ramp of dusty ochre plaster, concrete grey, maroon door paint and black line
identity_anchors.NOTE_FIST: a fist-sized stack of pale rectangular pixel rent-notes held in the owner's left hand, each note one chunky 24px block, countable at a glance
identity_anchors.PHONE: a plain dark slab phone held in the owner's right hand, its screen a single flat unlit rectangle with no markings, edges clean, left deliberately blank for compositing
identity_anchors.RENTOK_MARK: the supplied RentOK wordmark file placed unaltered — Rent in white, Ok in cyan #03FFF1, on a blue #0038FF ground — never redrawn, recoloured or regenerated

hero_frame.description: The owner three steps below the top landing, feet planted, shot from the same angle and the same stretch of handrail as beat 2 — the stairwell behind and below him now blank ochre plaster where five doors used to be — and in his raised right hand the phone showing five cyan tick-rows stacked in exactly the positions the five doors occupied. The corridor of problems is now a list in his hand.

audio.music_bed: Original chiptune in two states. Beats 1–5: a minor-key 8-bit loop at 96 bpm, square lead over a dragging bass, with a dull two-frame damage blip each time a note leaves the fist and paper-shuffle noise under the register pit. 13.5 s: the loop cuts to one held sine under the freeze. 18.2 s: the same melody in major at 132 bpm, one short cyan tick per door, arriving on the first door he walks through rather than on the thumb-press. 23.5 s: a two-note brand sting as the flag opens, then the loop resolves and holds under the card.

beats.title: Falling off his own stairs
beats.feeling: Recognition with a wince — a man who has not had a clean morning in months, caught at the exact second it goes wrong again.
beats.framing: PG_STAIRWELL ground-floor flight, camera locked side-on to the stairs, OWNER in the lower third, the first landing and its doorway-creature occupying the middle third above him. The handrail runs bottom-left to top-right. Through one open door behind him a steel double-bunk; a rack of rubber slippers on the landing; a room-number whiteboard beside the stair. HUD top-right, just under the safe band: NOTE_FIST's dues meter as a countable stack of pixel notes; HUD top-left: RENTOK_MARK small, as the cartridge mark. The doorway-creature is a maroon door with a latch for a mouth and a blank charcoal signboard plate bolted across its lintel, empty of any marking. Movement: the creature's latch-mouth snaps shut; the OWNER's body falls backwards; one note peels upward out of the fist.
beats.first_frame: The OWNER caught mid-fall backwards off the third stair, reading glasses knocked off his forehead and hanging in the air beside him, NOTE_FIST in his left hand with the top three notes already peeling away upward out of the fist. No title card, no start screen, no mark on the level itself.
beats.impact: Static locked camera, no move — the fall supplies all the motion. The clip holds three seconds because the signboard string must be read once. Sound: the loop is already running when the film starts, and one dull two-frame damage blip lands as the note leaves the fist, before the viewer has worked out what is being lost.

beats.title: The fifth of the month
beats.feeling: Being outnumbered by your own building — the specific fatigue of asking the same eleven people for the same thing.
beats.framing: First-floor landing, same handrail entering bottom-left, camera drifting up at the stair pitch. The doorway-creature here is a door with too many keyholes, its charcoal signboard plate blank across the lintel. A row of numbered room doors recedes up the flight above; each opens two pixels and shuts as the OWNER passes, and each time one shuts a note is tugged out of NOTE_FIST and vanishes into the gap. OWNER climbing right of centre, HUD meter top-right losing a note per door.
beats.first_frame: The OWNER's knuckles at a room door, mid-knock, the door already opening two pixels and a single note being drawn out of NOTE_FIST edge-on through the crack — his other hand still raised to knock at the next one.
beats.impact: One slow upward camera drift motivated by the climb itself, no cut inside the beat; the doors fire in rhythm with the bass so the losses feel metronomic rather than dramatic. The HUD meter drops three notes here, on frames where nothing else in the picture moves, so it stays countable at thumb size.

beats.title: The runner
beats.feeling: The drop in the stomach — not anger, the particular helplessness of watching money walk down your own stairs.
beats.framing: Second-floor landing. The doorway-creature is a door standing open onto nothing, blank signboard plate across its lintel. A tenant sprite in a backpack and slides crosses the landing right to left and drops clean out of the bottom of frame with a tin suitcase; the OWNER is caught mid-reach at the handrail, upper third. NOTE_FIST loses its single thickest note, which detaches and flutters down after the tenant, still visible for half a second at the bottom edge.
beats.first_frame: The tenant sprite already half out of the bottom of the frame, only head, backpack and the lifted tin suitcase still inside it, and the thickest note in NOTE_FIST detached and hanging a hand's width from the owner's fingers.
beats.impact: Static camera, deliberately refusing to follow him down — the frame keeps the empty doorway instead, which is the point. Screen direction holds: everything in this film travels up, so the one thing that travels down is the loss. Sound: the loop drops out for six frames and a descending three-note fall carries it, so with sound off the falling note carries the same information.

beats.title: The register pit
beats.feeling: Sinking — the airless feeling of a paper record that has stopped agreeing with itself.
beats.framing: Third-floor landing. The doorway-creature is a door built out of stacked register pages, blank signboard plate across the lintel; as the OWNER steps onto the landing the pages give way and the floor becomes a pit of loose ruled sheets. He sinks to the knee, centre frame, arms out, still holding NOTE_FIST and PHONE. Behind him, two half-visible columns of ruled lines drift out of alignment with each other. His climb rate visibly halves.
beats.first_frame: The OWNER knee-deep in loose ruled register pages, one hand still on the handrail, the page surface closed around his shins like water, a single sheet lifted and hanging beside his face.
beats.impact: The camera stops drifting for the first time in the film and holds dead still — the only stalled beat, which is what the problem feels like. Held two and a half seconds, the length it takes to read the slab and see him fail to move. Sound: the loop thins to bass and paper-shuffle noise fills the gap.

beats.title: The bell swarm
beats.feeling: Being pecked to death by small things — no single one serious, all of them at once.
beats.framing: Fourth-floor landing, the terrace flight visible above and out of reach. The doorway-creature is a door carrying a swarm of bell-pushes, blank signboard plate across its lintel; the bell-pushes detach and orbit the OWNER's head as small blinking pixel squares, one per room. He swats, covers his head, and loses the stair he had gained. The terrace light spills down the last flight behind him, unreachable.
beats.first_frame: The OWNER one step from the top of the fourth flight with eleven small blinking bell-pushes already orbiting his head and shoulders, his free arm across his face, one heel slipping backwards off the stair edge.
beats.impact: Slight camera push toward him as the swarm closes, the only inward move in the first half — it crowds the frame in the same way the swarm crowds him. Ends on the step he loses, with the dues meter at its lowest, so the film arrives at its worst point at 13.5 s of 30, exactly halfway.

beats.title: The cheat code
beats.feeling: The held breath of a pause button — then the small private satisfaction of knowing something the level does not.
beats.framing: The entire world freezes on one held frame: the OWNER stopped mid-fall on the fourth flight, plaster dust motionless in the air, the swarm hanging still, the HUD notes halfway out of the stack. Camera then pushes in on his right hand alone until PHONE fills most of the frame width. PHONE's screen is a single flat unlit rectangle in the generated still; it lights to flat blue #0038FF, and code composites the cheat-code entry bar across it. Nothing else in the frame moves for the whole beat except his thumb.
beats.first_frame: The frozen stairwell with every element stopped mid-motion — dust, notes, bell-pushes, the owner's falling body — and one thing alive in it: his right thumb, already descending, a pixel-width above the dark phone screen.
beats.impact: The freeze is carried by sound, not by a visual effect: the loop cuts to a single held sine so the viewer knows the game has been paused before the picture explains it. Then one bright rising install chime on the thumb-press, and blue #0038FF floods the phone — the first saturated colour in the film, held near-macro so that cyan will read later at any size. The music does not turn yet.

beats.title: The run
beats.feeling: Unbotheredness — the specific pleasure of walking through something that used to stop you.
beats.framing: The OWNER climbs the full stairwell again from the fourth flight upward, unhurried, not fighting. He walks straight through each doorway-creature; at contact each door collapses inward and becomes a single cyan #03FFF1 tick-row that files itself down onto PHONE's screen in his raised right hand. Five doors, five rows, in the order they were met. Behind him the stairwell is left blank ochre plaster. The HUD dues meter refills note by note. At 22.6 s the camera settles into the beat-2 angle on the same stretch of handrail for the hero frame.
beats.first_frame: The OWNER's shoulder already inside the first doorway-creature, the door's near edge breaking into a horizontal cyan row that has begun to travel down his arm toward the phone, his face entirely calm and his feet still walking.
beats.impact: One continuous upward move matched to his pace — no cutting inside the beat, so the run reads as one uninterrupted release after eleven seconds of interruption. The major-key version of the loop enters on the first door, not on the install, so the music follows the feeling the picture has already made. One short cyan tick per door. The beat ends on the hero frame held for three-quarters of a second with nothing moving in it.

beats.title: The flag
beats.feeling: Arrival without triumphalism — a working morning that finished on time, for once.
beats.framing: Terrace. The first and only open sky in the film, early dawn, a roofline of water tanks and dish antennas behind. The OWNER walks into the lower third and puts one hand on the flagpole. RENTOK_MARK is the flag itself — the supplied wordmark file, placed unaltered — snapping open left to right at the top of the long axis, opposite the owner at the bottom of it. PHONE still in his other hand, its five cyan rows visible small. Nothing else on the terrace.
beats.first_frame: The flag still furled tight against the pole at the top of the frame, the OWNER's hand just closing on the pole at the bottom of it, the sky behind them flat pale gold and completely empty.
beats.impact: Static camera; the only movement is the flag opening, so the mark is the single visual event in the frame. A two-note brand sting as it opens. The wide sky is held back until this beat precisely so that arriving at it feels like getting out of the stairwell, which is what the film has been about.

beats.title: Brand close
beats.feeling: A plain instruction from someone who has just shown you the point, with nothing asked of you but the obvious next move.
beats.framing: Code-composed card, no generated imagery. Flat blue #0038FF ground filling the frame. RENTOK_MARK centred in the upper middle third, unaltered. The ask beneath it in the middle third; the site line below that, smaller, still clear of the bottom safe band. The last frame of beat 8 does not dissolve — it cuts.
beats.first_frame: Flat #0038FF with the supplied wordmark already at full size and nothing else on screen yet; the ask and the site line land one beat later.
beats.impact: Hard cut from the flag, no dissolve and no fade — the film has no languid or sombre passage to justify one. The chiptune loop resolves and holds two seconds under the card. This is the pack frame the film ends on.

slab_verification.why: Composited onto the blank charcoal signboard plate of the first doorway-creature, which exists in the generated still only as an empty dark rectangle. The plate is the measured ground, so contrast is read on flat charcoal rather than on moving pixel art, and the string names the obstacle the picture is already showing rather than explaining it.

slab_rent.why: Same blank plate device on the second door. It enters four-tenths of a second after the cut so the picture establishes the action first and the label confirms it — never more than one string on screen at a time, and never more than three words before 13.5 s.

slab_runner.why: On the third door's plate, held while the tenant sprite leaves frame. This is the string the whole first half is building to, so it sits over the beat with the largest single loss in it.

slab_register.why: On the fourth door's plate, above a frame that has stopped moving. The stalled camera gives this string the quietest ground in the film, which it needs because it is the least visual of the five problems.

slab_complaints.why: On the fifth door's plate. One word, the shortest string of the five, against the busiest frame of the five — the swarm — so the reading load falls as the picture load rises.

cheat_code_bar.why: Composited onto the flat #0038FF phone screen as the cheat-code entry, the two strings stacking on two lines as supplied with no reflow. This is the film's only instruction before the card, and it is delivered as the game's own cheat entry rather than as an advertising super, which is what makes the mechanic and the ask the same act.

phone_rows.why: The five tick strings stamp onto the phone screen one per door as he walks through it, in the order the doors were met, each staying on screen until the card cut. By 22.6 s all five are stacked in the positions the five doors occupied — which is the hero frame, and the only place in the film where a benefit is stated in words.

brand_card.why: The ask, repeated in the customer's supplied second occurrence, now outside the game world and in plain instruction form under the mark, with the site line beneath it. Nothing else is on the card; the film's last two seconds do one job.

mandatory.customer_words: The video has a Mario game. The player is basically a PG owner.
mandatory.realisation: The whole thirty seconds is one original 16-bit platform level and the playable character is the paying-guest owner himself — a forty-five-year-old man in a half-sleeve checked shirt with his reading glasses on his forehead, present in every beat from frame one to the flag.
Beat 1: a doorway-creature with a latch for a mouth on the ground-floor landing, snapping shut on him, its signboard plate carrying the supplied string; answered in beat 7 by the ✓ DIGITAL KYC row.
Beat 2: the too-many-keyholes door and a flight of numbered room doors that each open two pixels, take a note out of his fist and shut; answered in beat 7 by the ✓ AUTOPAY row.

Beat 3: a door standing open onto nothing, a tenant sprite dropping out of the bottom of frame with a tin suitcase, and the thickest note in the owner's fist detaching and fluttering after him; answered in beat 7 by the ✓ DUES TRACKED LIVE row.

Beat 4: a door built of stacked register pages that gives way into a pit of loose ruled sheets he sinks into to the knee, with two columns of ruled lines drifting out of alignment behind him; answered in beat 7 by the ✓ ONE DASHBOARD row.
Beat 5: a door carrying a swarm of bell-pushes that detach and orbit his head, one per room, costing him the stair he had gained; answered in beat 7 by the ✓ COMPLAINT TICKETS row.

mandatory.customer_words: The game also introduces a cheat code — install RentOK app.
mandatory.realisation: Beat 6: on the hit that would end the run the world freezes on one held frame and the only thing that moves is his thumb on the phone; the phone screen lights to #0038FF and the cheat-code entry composited on it is the supplied INSTALL / RENTOK APP. The card in beat 9 repeats it as a plain instruction.

mandatory.customer_words: Once it is done, Mario gets a gun sort of power/immunity.
mandatory.realisation: Beat 7: immunity is shown, not a weapon. He walks through every doorway-creature untouched and unhurried, and nothing is fired — the power granted is that the doors no longer stop him. Declared as a deviation from the literal 'gun' so the exaggeration rests on the product's actual truth.

mandatory.customer_words: It runs and kills all the obstacles
mandatory.realisation: Beat 7: each of the five doors is destroyed at contact — it collapses inward and becomes a single cyan tick-row that files itself onto the phone screen. All five are cleared in the order they were met, and the stairwell behind him is left blank plaster.
Beat 8: the terrace flagpole, his hand closing on it, and the flag snapping open — the flag being the supplied RentOK wordmark file itself, placed unaltered, against the film's first open sky.

mandatory.customer_words: An original Mario-inspired game, rather than an exact reproduction of Nintendo's character, artwork, music or game assets.
mandatory.realisation: The hero is an Indian PG owner in ordinary clothes, the world is a four-storey paying-guest stairwell rather than a landscape, the level runs vertically rather than laterally, the obstacles are doors rather than creatures of the original, the music is an original chiptune written for this film, and the negative_line on every prompt explicitly excludes Nintendo characters, costumes, artwork, fonts, assets, coins and mushrooms.

Nine contiguous beats, 0 to 30.0 s, the last a code-composed card of clip_s 0. Thirteen and a half seconds of problem, four and a half of the cheat code, five and a half of the run, four and a half of the flag, two of the card.

mandatory.customer_words: Platforms: Instagram Reels / Facebook and YouTube Shorts. aspect 9:16
mandatory.realisation: The vertical frame is justified by the level's own shape — a building climbed bottom-of-frame to top-of-frame — rather than by the platform, and the top 14 per cent and bottom 20 per cent are kept clear of anything that has to be read so the platforms' own interfaces never sit on a string.

mandatory.customer_words: Brand and product source: Official RentOK website, https://rentok.com; Rent in white, Ok in cyan #03FFF1, blue #0038FF ground
mandatory.realisation: The supplied wordmark file is placed unaltered in four roles and never redrawn: the HUD cartridge mark from frame one, the lit phone ground at 13.5 s, the terrace flag at 23.5 s, and the closing card. Cyan #03FFF1 and blue #0038FF appear nowhere in the film before the phone lights, so both brand values enter as the first saturated colour the viewer has seen.

All thirteen strings are composed by code at their supplied values with no reflow, onto grounds built for them — blank charcoal signboard plates on the doors, the flat #0038FF phone screen, and the closing card. No legible glyph exists in any generated still; every prompt's negative_line forbids letters and numerals.

brand_timeline.in_context: The mark is in the HUD as the cartridge mark from frame one and never lapses. It becomes the product in use at 13.5 s, when the phone screen lights to #0038FF and he installs the app, and stays in his hand for the rest of the film collecting the five cyan rows. It becomes the world's own object at 23.5 s, as the terrace flag. It is the last frame at 28.0 s. Four asset types — HUD mark, product screen in use, in-situ flag, closing card — so attribution does not rest on the card alone.
brand_timeline.spoken: Not spoken. The deliverable constraint permits no dialogue or voice-over, so the brand's audio share is carried by two non-verbal marks instead: the rising install chime at the thumb-press and the two-note brand sting as the flag opens. This is a declared deviation from the pack default that the name is spoken as well as shown.

last_frame: The code-composed card: flat blue #0038FF filling the 9:16 frame, the supplied RentOK wordmark unaltered in the upper middle third, INSTALL / RENTOK APP beneath it, RENTOK.COM smaller below that and clear of the bottom safe band. No game imagery, no character, nothing else.

deviations.from: and default, on : cartoons are below average at changing brand preference with adults (the fabric-softener pair is the group's strongest evidence), and a parade of fleeting impressions is 'entertaining but impotent'.
deviations.brief_clause: 'The video has a Mario game. The player is basically a PG owner. The obstacles in the game are basically the problems that owner faces — tenant verification, collecting rent, tenants leaving without paying rent, no place to do reconciliation, solving complaints and so on.' The animated game form and its five problem scenes are the brief's substance, not its decoration. Half the objection is designed out rather than taken: beats 1–5 are one unbroken match-cut climb up one stairwell, so the five problems read as one morning in one building rather than as a vignette parade. The cartoon half of the objection is accepted knowingly.

deviations.from: default, on : no analogies — readers do not complete the equation and the vehicle displaces the product, as the Rembrandt is mistaken for the thing being sold.
deviations.brief_clause: 'I want to make a video for RentOK. The video has a Mario game.' The film is an analogy by instruction. The exposure is answered by 's inseparability test rather than hidden: the power-up is the app performing its actual function — doors becoming recorded ledger rows — so the story cannot be retold without naming what did the recording. A star, a gun or a mushroom would have made RentOK the Rembrandt.

deviations.from: , and / defaults: the on-screen CTA is voiced in the same words, and the brand name is spoken as well as shown.
deviations.brief_clause: The deliverable's standing constraint — 'no dialogue or voice-over' — with motion.audio true. The audio channel carries brand through two designed non-verbal marks instead (install chime, flag sting), and the film is built to pass muted, which is also what 's own LIMIT says the corpus cannot advise on.

deviations.from: and default, on : one specific figure — a percentage, a time, a sum — beats generalities.
deviations.brief_clause: 'Brand and product source: Official RentOK website, https://rentok.com.' No verified performance figure is supplied by the source of record, and forbids inventing one. The specific is therefore carried by countable objects rather than digits — the rent-notes in the fist and the HUD meter, which lose and refill one note at a time — which also satisfies 's requirement that standing be quantified and legible to an outsider without making a claim.

deviations.from: default, on the arbitration of mla_0064 against : default no humour; only when a brief clause asks, and only if the register fits product and audience.
deviations.brief_clause: 'The video has a Mario game' — a comic form the customer has specified. The clause is recorded here as requires. The film is written to be recognisable rather than funny: there are no gags, the owner is never the butt of anything, and no joke carries the selling point. 's bound — very few can write funny, and the rest should not try — is respected by not trying.

deviations.from: and default, on gote_0053: a shot whose job is to be read holds for as long as describing its contents aloud takes; makes a shorter one a deviation.
deviations.brief_clause: 'Duration: 30 seconds' against five named obstacles plus a cheat code, a power run and a flag. Beats 3, 4 and 5 run 2.5 s each, under their describe-aloud time. They sit in a declared action passage, and the load is shifted off the picture: each carries one short string on a flat plate, one sound event, and no second read.

deviations.from: The brief's own literal power-up: 'Mario gets a gun sort of power/immunity.'
deviations.brief_clause: 'Power-up design: Delegated to the creative system, while preserving the requested game-style power/immunity mechanic.' The immunity mechanic is preserved exactly — he is untouchable and clears every obstacle — but no weapon appears, because on an exaggeration must rest on a truth and the product's truth is that the problems stop being fights, not that they are shot. Recorded here so the departure from the customer's word is visible rather than quietly dropped.
